issues.legal_issue: A rent-control court may examine the evidence bearing on a tenant’s denial of the landlord’s title to determine whether the denial is bona fide, without deciding the parties’ ultimate title.
material_facts: In the eviction proceeding, the tenant denied the landlord’s title and relied on an asserted superior owner’s claim.
The courts examined the evidence concerning the tenant’s denial to decide whether it was bona fide; they did not adjudicate the ultimate title to the premises.
issues.conclusion: The courts could scrutinise the evidence for the limited purpose of testing the bona fides of the denial, but could not thereby decide the question of title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a tenant is generally estopped during the tenancy from denying that the landlord had title when the tenancy began. The Court relied on Mangat Ram v. Sardar Meharban Singh and D. Satyanarayana v. P. Jagadish for the scope and limits of that estoppel. It accepted the principle in LIC of India v. India Automobiles & Co. that title is not to be decided in these proceedings, while distinguishing a limited inquiry into the bona fides of a denial from an adjudication of title.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding was brought to determine eviction under a rent-control regime.
predicates.tenant_denied_landlord_title: The tenant disputed the title of the person seeking rent or eviction.
predicates.court_examined_evidence_of_denial: The court considered evidence relating to the tenant’s reasons and conduct in denying the landlord’s title.

issues.definition: When a tenant disputes a landlord’s title in a rent-control eviction proceeding and the court examines evidence of that denial, the court may test whether the denial is bona fide without deciding title.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s denial of the landlord’s title is not bona fide, and withholding rent amounts to wilful default, where the tenant was inducted by the landlord or the landlord’s predecessor, the tenant claims that a superior owner held title from the outset, and there is no evidence of a later loss of the landlord’s title.
material_facts: The tenant entered the premises under the landlord’s predecessor and paid rent to that predecessor and later to the landlord.
The tenant stopped paying rent to the landlord after asserting that a religious institution owned the premises from the beginning.
The institution had not demanded rent from the tenant or informed the tenant that it owned the premises; the tenant himself asked the institution to recognise him as its tenant.
There was no evidence that the landlord lost title after the tenant’s induction.

The institution later sued asserting paramount title, and an affidavit describing the landlord as its lessee concerned a different relationship and did not determine the landlord-tenant relationship in the rent-control proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The denial of title was not bona fide, and the tenant’s failure to pay rent to the landlord was wilful default.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, estops a tenant from denying the landlord’s title at the beginning of the tenancy, however defective that title may be. As explained in Mangat Ram v. Sardar Meharban Singh and D. Satyanarayana v. P. Jagadish, the estoppel does not bar a tenant from asserting that the landlord’s title later ended when a paramount title-holder threatens eviction. Here, the tenant asserted that the superior owner held title from the outset, and there was no evidence of a later loss of title. Section 2(6) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, broadly defines a landlord to include a person receiving or entitled to receive rent; its explanation also treats a tenant who sublets as a landlord in relation to the subtenant. The landlord’s separate relationship with a superior owner did not displace the landlord-tenant relationship at issue.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_was_inducted_by_landlord_or_predecessor and tenant_paid_rent_to_landlord and tenant_claimed_superior_owner_had_title_from_inception and no_evidence_of_later_loss_of_landlord_title and superior_owner_never_demanded_rent_or_asserted_ownership_to_tenant and tenant_withheld_rent_from_landlord

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding sought eviction under a rent-control regime.
predicates.tenant_was_inducted_by_landlord_or_prede: The tenant entered the premises through the person seeking rent or that person’s predecessor.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_to_landlord: The tenant had paid rent to the person seeking rent.
predicates.tenant_claimed_superior_owner_had_title_: The tenant based the denial on a claim that another person owned the premises from the start of the tenancy.
predicates.no_evidence_of_later_loss_of_landlord_ti: No evidence showed that the person seeking rent lost title after the tenant’s induction.
predicates.superior_owner_never_demanded_rent_or_as: The alleged superior owner had neither demanded rent from the tenant nor told the tenant that it owned the premises.
predicates.tenant_withheld_rent_from_landlord: The tenant stopped paying rent to the person who had received rent from the tenant.

issues.definition: When a tenant in a rent-control eviction proceeding was inducted by and paid rent to the landlord, claims a superior owner held title from the outset, has no evidence that the landlord later lost title, and withholds rent although the superior owner never demanded it or asserted ownership to the tenant, the denial is not bona fide and the withholding is wilful default.

issues.legal_issue: A superior owner’s suit asserting title does not by itself end the existing landlord-tenant relationship relevant to rent liability under the rent-control regime.
material_facts: The tenant had been inducted by the landlord’s predecessor and later paid rent to the landlord.
The tenant relied on a suit by a religious institution asserting paramount title and on an affidavit addressing the landlord’s relationship with that institution.
The landlord was not a party to that suit, and the asserted relationship between the landlord and the institution was distinct from the tenant’s relationship with the landlord.
The tenant raised the superior-title suit as a reason the eviction decree could not be executed.
issues.conclusion: The superior owner’s suit did not, merely by being filed, terminate the landlord-tenant arrangement or make the eviction decree inexecutable on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(6) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, defines landlord broadly to include a person receiving or entitled to receive rent, and its explanation includes a tenant as landlord in relation to a subtenant. The Court treated the relationships between the tenant and the rent-claiming landlord, and between that landlord and the alleged superior owner, as distinct; the latter relationship did not itself end the former.

predicates.rent_control_execution_challenge: The tenant challenged execution of an eviction order made in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.tenant_landlord_relationship_existed_bef: The tenant’s relationship with the person seeking rent was established before the superior owner brought suit.
predicates.superior_owner_suit_asserted_title: Another person brought a suit asserting paramount title to the premises.
predicates.landlord_was_not_party_to_superior_owner: The person seeking rent was not a party to the superior owner’s suit.

issues.definition: When execution of a rent-control eviction order is challenged on the basis of a later suit asserting paramount title, that suit does not itself end an already established tenant-landlord relationship if the landlord was not a party to it.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings that premises are required for demolition and reconstruction should stand when no material illegality is shown as a basis for disturbing them.
material_facts: The rent-control authorities concurrently found that the premises were required for demolition and reconstruction.
The High Court upheld those findings, and no illegality warranting their reversal was identified before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the premises were required for demolition and reconstruction was not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to interfere with concurrent findings of the rent-control authorities and the High Court when no material illegality had been shown.

predicates.appeal_challenges_rent_control_eviction_: The appeal challenges a finding made in a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_finding_of_reconstruction_req: The rent-control authorities reached the same finding that the premises were required for demolition and reconstruction.
predicates.no_material_illegality_shown: The challenging party identified no material illegality warranting reversal of the concurrent finding.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a rent-control finding, the authorities concur that the premises are required for demolition and reconstruction, and no material illegality is shown, the concurrent finding is upheld.
